title: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
summary: Send each prompt to the cheapest model that can answer it well: FrugalGPT-style cascades, RouteLLM's learned routers and their cost-quality metrics, Bedrock's managed routing, and how routers fail.
outcomes: Compute blended cost per million tokens for a given share of strong-model calls
Explain how a FrugalGPT cascade uses a scorer and per-tier thresholds, and what escalation costs in money and latency
Explain how RouteLLM trains a win-probability router from preference data and turns it into decisions with a threshold
Compute PGR and read APGR and CPT to compare routers at the operating point you need
Identify router drift, judge bias and router overhead, and configure Bedrock's fallback-based routing

lessons.title: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money

blocks.md:
Suppose your product sends every user prompt to the strongest model you can buy. Quality is high, and so is the bill. Chen, Zaharia and Zou (FrugalGPT, 2023) surveyed 12 commercial LLM APIs in March 2023 and found prices that differ by up to two orders of magnitude: processing 10 million input tokens cost USD 0.2 on GPT-J (via Textsynth) and USD 30 on GPT-4.

Their illustrative customer-service bot answers 360,000 queries a month with 1,800-token prompts and 80-token answers. At GPT-4's March 2023 prices (USD 0.03 per thousand input tokens, USD 0.06 per thousand output tokens) that is about USD 21.2K per month.

The waste is that many prompts do not need the strong model. "What is the capital of France?" gets the same answer from a small model. The RouteLLM paper (Ong et al., 2024) puts the gap at more than 50x for one model family (Claude 3 Haiku at USD 1.25 versus Claude 3 Opus at USD 75 per million output tokens) and estimates a **blended** price, mixing input and output tokens in the proportions of its training prompts (95 input, 264 output on average): about USD 24.7 per million tokens for GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106) and USD 0.24 for Mixtral 8x7B.

If a fraction $p$ of traffic goes to the strong model and the rest to the weak one, the blended cost is a weighted average:

blocks.caption: c_s and c_w are the strong and weak prices per million tokens. With a 100x price gap the strong term dominates: cost is roughly proportional to p, the share of strong calls.

scenes.caption: The two endpoints: GPT-4 at about 24.70 and Mixtral 8x7B at 0.24 USD per million tokens, a ratio of about 103x. These are the paper's 2024 estimates, used here only as a worked example.
Sending half the traffic to each model at random costs 0.5 x 24.70 + 0.5 x 0.24 = 12.47. Random mixing saves money but also loses quality on every hard prompt that lands on the weak model.
A router that sends only 30% of prompts to GPT-4 costs 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.58, about 3.3x cheaper than GPT-4 only. Whether quality survives depends on which 30% it picks.

blocks.md:
There are two ways to pick the model per prompt.

- **Routing** decides *before* generation. A small model called the **router** reads the prompt and sends it to exactly one LLM. One call per prompt.
- **Cascading** decides *after* generation. Call the cheap model first, judge its answer, and only if the answer looks unreliable call the next, more expensive model.

FrugalGPT groups cost-saving ideas into three families: prompt adaptation (shorter prompts), LLM approximation (caching answers, fine-tuning a cheaper model) and LLM cascades. This course covers cascades and routers; caching and prompt compression have their own course.

blocks.title: A router makes one decision before any LLM runs

scenes.caption: The router sits in front of both models. It sees only the prompt, never an answer, so its decision is a prediction about how much the strong model would help.
"What is the capital of France?": the router predicts the strong model would not do better, so the weak model answers. Cost for this prompt is about 1% of the strong model's.
"Find the race condition in this code": the router predicts a large quality gap, so the strong model answers. The user waits for one model only, plus the router's small overhead.

blocks.md: Routing pays off when two things are true at once: the price gap between models is large, and a sizable share of your prompts are ones where the weak model is just as good. If every prompt is hard, no router can save money without losing quality.

blocks.question: Using RouteLLM's blended prices (GPT-4 24.70, Mixtral 0.24 USD per million tokens), a router sends 30% of traffic to GPT-4. What is the blended cost per million tokens?
options: About 7.41, because only the GPT-4 share costs anything meaningful
About 12.47, the same as a 50/50 mix
About 7.58
About 17.36
blocks.explain: 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.41 + 0.168 = 7.58. Ignoring the weak model is a fine approximation here (7.41 is close) but not exact. 12.47 is the 50/50 mix and 17.36 corresponds to 70% strong.

blocks.question: Which statement correctly separates a router from a cascade?
options: A router calls every model and picks the best answer; a cascade calls one
A router chooses one model before generation; a cascade generates with a cheap model first and escalates only if the answer scores poorly
Both decide after generation, but a cascade uses a cheaper scorer
A router always costs more than a cascade because it runs a classifier
blocks.explain: Calling every model and picking the best answer is an ensemble (LLM-Blender does this), which costs the most. A router predicts from the prompt alone. A cascade sees an actual answer, which gives it more information but makes escalated prompts pay for several calls.

lessons.title: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure

blocks.md:
FrugalGPT's cascade has two parts. A **generation scoring function** $g(q, a)$ takes a query and an answer and returns a reliability score in $[0, 1]$. A **list** of $m$ APIs, ordered from cheap to expensive, has one threshold $\tau_i$ per tier. For each query the cascade calls tier 1, scores its answer, and returns it if the score is above $\tau_1$; otherwise it calls tier 2, and so on. The last tier's answer is always accepted.

The scorer is not an LLM. The paper trains a simple regression model that learns whether a generation is correct from the query and the answer; in its case study the scorer is a DistilBERT model, much smaller than any of the LLMs.

blocks.caption: z is the tier where the cascade stops. Every tier up to and including z is paid for, not just the one whose answer is returned.

blocks.md:
The list and the thresholds are learned together: maximize expected answer quality subject to an average cost budget. That is a mixed-integer problem, so FrugalGPT uses a specialized optimizer that prunes lists whose models rarely disagree.

On HEADLINES (classifying gold-price news headlines as up, down, neutral or none) with a budget of USD 6.5, one fifth of GPT-4's cost on that dataset, the learned cascade was: GPT-J, accept if the score is above 0.96; otherwise J1-L, accept if above 0.37; otherwise GPT-4. The paper reports 80% lower cost than GPT-4 with 1.5% higher accuracy. Across its datasets it reports matching the best single LLM with up to 98% cost reduction.

blocks.title: The cascade FrugalGPT learned on HEADLINES

scenes.caption: The learned strategy: three tiers and two thresholds. The thresholds are not equal; the optimizer set a very strict bar for GPT-J and a loose one for J1-L.
Query A: GPT-J's answer scores 0.98, above 0.96, so it is returned. Only the cheapest model and the tiny scorer ran. (Scores in these scenes are illustrative.)
Query B: GPT-J scores 0.41, so the cascade escalates. J1-L's answer scores 0.52, above 0.37, and is returned. This query paid for two LLM calls.
Query C: both cheap answers score low (0.12, then 0.20), so GPT-4 answers. This query paid for all three calls and waited for all three, which is the cascade's worst case.

blocks.title: Tracing query B through a cascade
blocks.code:
TIERS = [("gpt-j", 0.96), ("j1-large", 0.37), ("gpt-4", None)]

def cascade(query):
    spent = 0.0
    for model, tau in TIERS:
        answer = call(model, query)
        spent += price(model, query, answer)
        if tau is None:              # last tier: always accept
            return answer, model, spent
        score = scorer(query, answer)    # reliability in [0, 1]
        if score > tau:
            return answer, model, spent

scenes.caption: The tiers and thresholds come from the optimizer. The last tier has no threshold: whatever GPT-4 says is final.
Tier 1: GPT-J answers and we pay for it whether or not we keep the answer.
The scorer rates the answer 0.41. That is not above 0.96, so the loop moves on.
Tier 2: J1-L answers; its cost is added to what we already spent.
0.52 is above 0.37, so J1-L's answer is returned. GPT-4 never runs for this query.

blocks.md:
For a two-tier cascade where a fraction $e$ of queries escalate, expected cost per query is $c_w + e\,c_s$: the weak model runs on every query. A router that sends the same fraction $e$ to the strong model costs $e\,c_s + (1-e)\,c_w$.

Use RouteLLM's average request (95 input and 264 output tokens) and its prices: GPT-4 (USD 10 and USD 30 per million input and output tokens) costs about USD 8,870 per million queries, and Mixtral (USD 0.24 per million tokens) about USD 86.

blocks.prompt: With e = 30% of queries escalating, how much more does the cascade cost than a router that sends the same 30% to GPT-4? And what does the cascade cost in latency?
blocks.reveal:
Cost: the cascade costs 86 + 0.3 x 8,870 = about USD 2,747 per million queries; the router costs 0.3 x 8,870 + 0.7 x 86 = about USD 2,721. Under 1% apart, because the cheap model is nearly free.

Latency is the real price. Assume the weak model takes 0.6 s, the scorer 0.02 s, the strong model 2.0 s and a router 0.03 s. Every escalated query in the cascade waits 0.6 + 0.02 + 2.0 = 2.62 s. Mean latency is 0.7 x 0.62 + 0.3 x 2.62 = 1.22 s for the cascade versus 0.03 + 0.7 x 0.6 + 0.3 x 2.0 = 1.05 s for the router.

blocks.title: Latency: cascade escalation versus a router (assumed timings)

scenes.caption: An easy query in a cascade: the weak model answers in 0.6 s and the scorer accepts it 0.02 s later. This is as fast as using the weak model alone.
A hard query in a cascade: the weak answer is generated and rejected first, then the strong model starts at 0.62 s. The user waits 2.62 s.

The same hard query through a router: 0.03 s to classify the prompt, then the strong model. Done at 2.03 s. It skips the wasted weak call but never sees an answer, so it can err where a scorer would not. Timings are assumed, not measured.

blocks.md:
Why use a cascade at all, then? Because judging an answer is easier than predicting from the prompt alone whether the cheap model will cope. A scorer can notice that an answer is malformed, hedged or inconsistent. AutoMix (Aggarwal et al.) takes this further: the small model checks its own answer with few-shot self-verification, and a router decides whether to escalate based on that noisy confidence.

Cascades fit best when answers are short (labels, extractions, yes or no), when latency is not critical (batch jobs), or when a cheap check of correctness exists, such as a schema validator or unit tests for generated code.

A scorer is only as good as the data it was trained on. Thresholds like 0.96 were tuned on one dataset's training split. On a new kind of query an overconfident scorer accepts wrong cheap answers silently: cost goes down and nobody notices that quality went down too. Track the acceptance rate per tier and audit a sample of accepted answers.

blocks.question: You raise the tier-1 threshold of a two-tier cascade from 0.96 to 0.99. What happens?
options: Fewer queries escalate, so cost falls
More queries escalate: cost and mean latency rise, and accuracy usually rises because fewer weak answers are accepted
Nothing changes, since the scorer's outputs are calibrated probabilities
The weak model is skipped for hard queries, so latency falls
blocks.explain: A stricter threshold accepts fewer cheap answers, so more queries pay for the strong model and wait for both calls. The weak model still runs on every query; a cascade cannot skip it, only a router can.

blocks.question: Which workload is the best fit for a cascade rather than a router?
options: A voice assistant with a 300 ms latency budget
A chat product where most answers are long essays
A nightly batch that labels support tickets into 12 categories, where a wrong label is cheap to detect
Any workload, because cascades are always more accurate
blocks.explain: Short answers make the wasted weak call cheap, a batch job does not care about the extra latency, and an easy correctness check makes the scorer reliable. A tight latency budget punishes escalation, and long answers make the wasted weak generation expensive.

lessons.title: Learned routers: predict whether the strong model would win

blocks.md:
A router has to decide from the prompt alone. RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024, ICLR 2025) frames this as binary routing between a **strong** model class (high quality, high cost; GPT-4 in their main experiments) and a **weak** one (Mixtral 8x7B), with one LLM call per query.

The router has two parts. A **win prediction model** estimates $P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q)$, the probability that the strong model's answer to prompt $q$ would be preferred over the weak model's. A **cost threshold** $\alpha \in [0,1]$ turns that probability into a decision.

blocks.tex: R^{\alpha}(q) = \begin{cases} M_{weak} & \text{if } P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q) < \alpha \\ M_{strong} & \text{if } P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q) \ge \alpha \end{cases}
blocks.caption: A higher alpha sends more traffic to the weak model (cheaper); a lower alpha favors the strong model. One trained router gives a whole family of operating points.

blocks.md:
The parameters $\theta$ are fit by maximum likelihood on **preference data**: triples of a prompt and a label saying whether the strong model won, the weak model won, or it was a tie.

The main source is about 80K battles from Chatbot Arena, where users compare two anonymous models and vote. Labels between any two specific models are sparse (under 0.1% of pairs), so the authors cluster 64 models into 10 tiers by Arena score, take the top two tiers as strong and the third as weak, and keep only who won. After pruning prompts shorter than 16 characters, 65K comparisons remain.

blocks.title: One router, four thresholds (toy prompts, illustrative scores)

scenes.caption: Ten toy prompts with the router's predicted win probability. At alpha = 0.8 only the race-condition bug goes to the strong model (S): 10% strong calls, blended cost 2.69 USD per million tokens.
alpha = 0.6 adds the proof and the tax calculation: 30% strong calls, cost 7.58.
alpha = 0.4 adds the SQL window query: 40% strong, cost 10.02. The router's ranking stays fixed; alpha only moves the cut.
alpha = 0.2 adds the regex, the summary and the idiom: 70% strong, cost 17.36. If the summary and idiom gain nothing from the strong model, those two calls are pure waste.

blocks.md:
Sparse human votes are not enough, especially for prompts unlike Arena's. RouteLLM augments the data two ways:

- **Golden labels**: about 1,500 MMLU validation questions. Each model's answer is compared to the answer key, which yields a win, loss or tie for free.
- **LLM-judge labels**: prompts from the Nectar dataset that already had GPT-4 responses, new Mixtral responses, and GPT-4 as a pairwise judge. About 120K samples for roughly USD 700 in total.

The judge part is the LLM-as-judge setup from the prerequisite course, used here to manufacture routing labels.

The paper compares four ways to parameterize $P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q)$:

1. **Similarity-weighted ranking**: embed the new prompt, weight every training prompt by its similarity to it (weight $\gamma^{1 + S}$ with $\gamma = 10$), then fit Bradley-Terry strengths for strong and weak on the weighted battles. No training; the fit happens at inference time.
2. **Matrix factorization**: learn a score $\delta(M, q)$ from a model embedding and a query embedding; $P = \sigma(\delta(M_s, q) - \delta(M_w, q))$.
3. **BERT classifier**: fine-tune BERT-base with a logistic head on the CLS token.
4. **Causal LLM classifier**: fine-tune Llama 3 8B to emit the label as a next token.

The first two embed prompts with OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small.

Step back and you can see three families of **router signals**, whoever builds the router:

- **Prompt classifiers** (BERT, causal LLM, matrix factorization): read the prompt, predict difficulty or the win probability. Cheap and pre-generation.
- **Similarity to past prompts**: look up prompts you have already seen with known outcomes, as in similarity-weighted ranking or a k-nearest-neighbor vote. Needs an embedding call and an index.
- **Judge or confidence on an answer**: score a cheap model's actual output, as in FrugalGPT's scorer or AutoMix's self-verification. More information, but only available after a generation, which makes it a cascade.

Treat alpha as a cost knob, not a quality guarantee. The predicted probabilities are rarely well calibrated, so choose alpha on a held-out set from your own traffic: pick the value that gives the share of strong calls (and hence the cost) you can afford, then measure quality at that point.

blocks.question: RouteLLM's routers trained only on Chatbot Arena data performed close to a random router on MMLU and GSM8K, but well on MT Bench. What is the most likely explanation?
options: MMLU and GSM8K are too easy for the strong model
The test prompts are unlike the training prompts, so the win predictor has not learned their difficulty
The routers were not given enough GPU memory at inference
Random routing is optimal for multiple-choice questions
blocks.explain: The paper attributes it to most MMLU questions being out of distribution for Arena data. Adding about 1,500 golden-labeled MMLU validation questions, under 2% of the training data, made every router beat random on MMLU.

blocks.question: Which RouteLLM router does its fitting at inference time instead of during training?
options: The causal LLM classifier
Matrix factorization
The BERT classifier
Similarity-weighted ranking
blocks.explain: Similarity-weighted ranking solves a weighted Bradley-Terry problem for each new prompt, weighting training battles by similarity. That is why it needs no training, and also why it was the slowest router to serve.

lessons.title: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT

blocks.md:
A router has two numbers that pull against each other. RouteLLM measures **cost** as $c$, the percentage of calls sent to the strong model, and **quality** as $r$, the average response score on a benchmark (accuracy on MMLU, a 1 to 10 judge rating on MT Bench).

Because a router's quality always lies between the weak model's and the strong model's, the paper normalizes it as the **performance gap recovered**:

blocks.caption: PGR = 1 means the router matches the strong model; 0 means it matches the weak one. APGR averages PGR across ten cost levels, which is the area under the PGR versus strong-call-share curve.

blocks.md:
Neither number works alone: a router that always picks the strong model has PGR = 1 and saves nothing. So the paper sweeps $\alpha$, plots PGR against the share of strong calls, and reports two summaries:

- **APGR**, the area under that curve. A router that routes at random gets about 0.5, because on average a random $c\%$ of strong calls recovers $c\%$ of the gap.
- **CPT(x%)**, the call-performance threshold: the minimum share of strong calls needed to reach a PGR of x%. Lower is better.

blocks.title: PGR versus share of strong calls (simplified curve family)

x.label: % of calls to the strong model

scenes.caption: With k = 1 the curve is the diagonal: a random router. CPT(50%) = 50% and APGR = 0.5. This curve family is a simplified stand-in, not a fit to real data.
k = 2.5: the router sends the prompts that gain most from the strong model first, so PGR rises quickly. CPT(50%) falls to 24.2% and APGR is 0.714.
k = 5: CPT(50%) is 12.9% and APGR 0.833, close to what RouteLLM's best MT Bench router reports (CPT(50%) of 13.40%, APGR 0.802).

blocks.md:
Now do it by hand on the ten toy prompts from the last lesson. Each prompt has a quality score for the weak and for the strong model (1 to 10, invented for this example). Averages: weak 6.5, strong 8.4, a gap of 1.9 points. Sweeping $\alpha$:

- $\alpha$ = 0.8: 10% strong, average 7.0, PGR 0.263, blended cost 2.69
- $\alpha$ = 0.6: 30% strong, average 7.6, PGR 0.579, cost 7.58
- $\alpha$ = 0.4: 40% strong, average 8.0, PGR 0.789, cost 10.02
- $\alpha$ = 0.2: 70% strong, average 8.3, PGR 0.947, cost 17.36

Costs are USD per million tokens with RouteLLM's blended prices (24.70 strong, 0.24 weak). At $\alpha$ = 0.4 you keep 79% of the quality gap for 41% of the GPT-4-only price.

blocks.title: Toy router: blended USD per 1M tokens at each threshold

scenes.caption: Cost falls almost linearly with the share of strong calls, because the weak model is about 100x cheaper. All strong: 24.70; all weak: 0.24.
Same thresholds, now showing PGR x 100 (share of the quality gap kept). Quality falls slowly at first and then fast: the last prompts moved to the weak model are the ones that needed the strong one.

blocks.prompt: Your quality target is PGR of at least 80% on the toy set. Which alpha do you choose, and what does it cost?
blocks.reveal: alpha = 0.4 gives PGR 0.789, just short of 0.80, so you must go down to alpha = 0.2: PGR 0.947 at 70% strong calls and 17.36 USD per million tokens. On a ten-prompt set the CPT curve moves in big steps; on real traffic you would search alpha finely on a large held-out set. Notice how much the last 1% of target costs: from 10.02 to 17.36.

blocks.md:
What did RouteLLM measure? On MT Bench routing between GPT-4 and Mixtral 8x7B, a random router has CPT(50%) of 49.03%, CPT(80%) of 78.08% and APGR 0.500. The matrix factorization router trained on Arena plus judge-labeled data reaches CPT(50%) of 13.40%, CPT(80%) of 31.31% and APGR 0.802. The BERT router trained on Arena data alone scored APGR 0.391, worse than random, which the authors attribute to a large model in a low-data regime.

The paper converts this into cost savings over GPT-4: 3.66x on MT Bench at CPT(50%) (95% of GPT-4's quality), but 1.41x on MMLU and 1.49x on GSM8K. The same routers, without retraining, also beat random when the pair was swapped to Claude 3 Opus and Sonnet or to Llama 3.1 70B and 8B (best APGR 0.772 and 0.767).

Read router claims carefully. "2x cheaper at the same quality" depends on the benchmark, the model pair, the quality target and the baseline. RouteLLM's savings are the random router's share of strong calls divided by the best router's at the same PGR (GPT-4 cost dominates), not a comparison with a GPT-4-only deployment, and vary from 1.41x to 3.66x across three benchmarks. Only an evaluation on your own prompts tells you what you will get.

blocks.question: A router has r = 7.6 on a benchmark where the weak model scores 6.5 and the strong model 8.4. What is its PGR?
blocks.explain: PGR = (7.6 - 6.5) / (8.4 - 6.5) = 1.1 / 1.9 = 0.579. 0.905 is 7.6 / 8.4, which ignores the weak baseline; 0.421 is 1 minus the right answer.

blocks.question: Router A has APGR 0.80. Router B has APGR 0.75 but needs fewer strong calls than A to reach PGR 95%. Your product must stay at 95% of the strong model's quality gap. Which router should you prefer?
options: A, because APGR summarizes everything
Neither, because APGR below 0.9 is unusable
B, because what matters is the cost at your operating point, here CPT(95%)
A, because a higher area always means lower cost at every point
blocks.explain: APGR averages over all cost levels, most of which you will never run at. Curves can cross, so the router that is better on average can be worse at the one operating point you care about. RouteLLM reports CPT at specific targets for this reason.

lessons.title: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail

blocks.md:
You do not have to train a router yourself. Amazon Bedrock **Intelligent Prompt Routing** is documented as "a single serverless endpoint to efficiently route requests between different foundational models within the same model family". For each request it predicts the response quality of each model from the prompt and routes to the one with the best combination of quality and cost. The response says which model handled it.

There are **default prompt routers**, preconfigured by AWS, and **configured prompt routers**. When you configure one, the docs say you must choose exactly two models within the same family, a **fallback model**, and a **routing criterion**: the response quality difference.

The fallback model is the anchor. In the docs' example, with a response quality difference of 10% and Amazon Nova Lite as the fallback, the router switches to the other model (say Nova Pro) only if its predicted response quality is more than 10% better than Nova Lite's.

The documented limitations matter as much as the features: routing is optimized only for English prompts, it cannot adjust decisions using application-specific performance data, and it may not route optimally for unique or specialized use cases because its effectiveness depends on its initial training data. AWS's product page claims routing "can reduce costs by up to 30% without compromising on accuracy"; that is AWS's own claim, not a measured result you can assume for your traffic. The supported model list varies by Region and changes over time, so check the docs.

blocks.caption: Creating a configured router with the AWS CLI (placeholders in angle brackets). The CreatePromptRouter API takes fallbackModel as a single object; the user guide's example wraps it in a list. GetPromptRouter, ListPromptRouters and DeletePromptRouter manage it afterwards.

blocks.title: A configured router with Nova Lite as fallback (10% criterion)

scenes.caption: Prompt 1 is a simple rewording task. The router predicts Nova Pro would be only 4% better (illustrative; AWS does not document the predictor's internals).
4% is below the 10% criterion, so the request goes to the fallback model. The response carries the id of the model that answered, which you should log.
Prompt 2 is a multi-step proof. The router predicts Nova Pro would be 25% better.
25% clears the criterion, so Nova Pro answers. One model call per request, as in RouteLLM; the router's own work happens before the call.

blocks.md:
**Failure mode 1: router drift.** A router learns the difficulty of the prompts it was trained on. RouteLLM's Arena-trained routers were near or below random on MMLU and GSM8K, and the paper found router quality tracked a benchmark-dataset similarity score. In production the drift comes from you: a new feature, a new language, a new customer segment, or swapping in newer models. Bedrock's English-only optimization is the same issue stated up front.

Watch the share of strong calls over time (a sudden change means the input distribution moved) and keep auditing a sample of weak-model answers against the strong model.

**Failure mode 2: judge bias in the labels.** When routing labels come from an LLM judge, the router learns what the judge prefers. Zheng et al. (2023), who introduced MT Bench and studied GPT-4 as a judge, document position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. A router trained on such labels can learn "send it to the model that writes longer answers" rather than "send it to the model that is right". RouteLLM followed that paper's debiasing practices; mix in labels you trust (golden answers, human votes) and evaluate on them.

**Failure mode 3: the router's own cost and latency.** RouteLLM measured serving costs: matrix factorization handled 155.16 requests per second on one NVIDIA L4 GPU (USD 3.32 per million requests), while similarity-weighted ranking managed 2.9 per second on a CPU-only n2-standard-8 VM (USD 39.26 per million). Even the most expensive added at most 0.4% to GPT-4 generation cost. Latency is different: the embedding call and classifier sit before the first token of every request.

Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

blocks.question: A Bedrock router uses Nova Lite as fallback with a 10% response quality difference. For a prompt, Nova Pro's predicted quality is 6% better than Nova Lite's. Which model answers?
options: Nova Pro, because it is predicted to be better
Both, and the router returns the better answer
Nova Lite, because 6% does not exceed the 10% criterion
Neither: the request fails and must be retried
blocks.explain: The criterion sets how much better the other model must be predicted to be before the router leaves the fallback. 6% is below 10%, so Nova Lite answers. Bedrock calls one model per request; it does not generate both and compare.

blocks.question: After launching in Japan, your router's share of strong-model calls drops from 35% to 12% and complaints about answer quality rise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The strong model became cheaper
Input distribution shift: the router misjudges the difficulty of prompts unlike its training data and sends hard ones to the weak model
Judge bias toward longer answers
The router's GPU is overloaded
blocks.explain: A sudden change in routing mix plus worse quality right after new traffic arrives points to drift. Bedrock's docs say its routing is optimized only for English prompts, and RouteLLM's routers fell to near random on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

blocks.question: Your router's training labels come from an LLM judge, and you notice it sends almost every prompt that asks for a list to the strong model. Which fix targets the likely cause?
options: Add trusted labels (golden answers or human votes) and evaluate the router on them, controlling for answer length
Lower alpha so more prompts reach the strong model
Replace the router with a cascade
Use a larger embedding model
blocks.explain: If the judge prefers longer, more detailed answers (verbosity bias), the router learns to route on length-related features. Trusted labels and an evaluation that controls for length expose and correct that. Moving alpha only shifts the cut; it does not fix what the router learned.
